177.subtitle: The scarlet flower, the girl, and the woman of the house

commentary.meaning: Seven names, and not one of them metaphysical. The verse opens with her colour, matched to the scarlet of the bandhūka, a flower that opens at midday and is finished by evening; then it calls her a girl; then it says that what she does with the world is play. The second line is four names in a row beginning with su-, good or well, and every one of them belongs to the vocabulary of the household rather than of doctrine: the woman in whom every auspicious sign is present, the maker of ease, the one richly dressed, and finally the suvāsinī, the honoured woman of the house. Six verses from the end of a thousand names one might expect the hymn to climb. Instead it comes down into the domestic room and stays there. The last word of this verse is also the first word of the next, where the sense in which she is a suvāsinī will be made ritually explicit, and the two verses have to be read as one movement.
commentary.history:
The bandhūka is Pentapetes phoenicea, called in English the noon flower or scarlet mallow, and its habit is part of what the name conveys: the flowers open around midday and are spent by the following morning. Sanskrit poets use it as a standard measure of a particular red, not the pale flush of dawn and not the deep red of the pomegranate blossom but a saturated scarlet. Prakhyā, from pra-√khyā, to become visible, means look or appearance, and the compound is a bahuvrīhi — she whose look is that of the bandhūka flower. Redness is not ornamental in this tradition. It is the colour under which she is visualised in the meditation verses that precede the recitation, the colour of aruṇa, of the sun just risen, and of desire understood as the productive force of the world rather than as a private appetite. The hymn has reached for other red flowers earlier; here the comparison returns at exactly the point where the vocabulary begins to shift from cosmology to the ordinary.

Bālā does two things at once. It is the plain Sanskrit word for a girl who has not grown up. It is also, in this school, the name of a deity and of her mantra: Bālā, or Bālā Tripurasundarī, whose formula is short — commonly given as three syllables against the fifteen of the principal vidyā — and who is in many lineages the first mantra an initiate receives. Traditions differ on how she stands to Lalitā, some describing her as a daughter, others as Lalitā herself in a younger form, and the disagreement is not one the sources try to settle. What matters for reading the name here is that a large part of the tradition's beginning practice hangs on this single word. It is also worth noticing that the very next verse will call her pūrvajā, born before everything. Girl and elder of the world, two lines apart, and no commentator treats this as a problem needing a solution.

Līlā is play, and it is the standard Indian answer to the question of why a being that lacks nothing should act at all. If creation met a need it would not be the act of a complete being; if it were compelled it would not be free; so it is called play, which is activity without motive outside itself. Vinodinī sharpens this. Vinoda is diversion or amusement, from vi-√nud, to push away — literally what pushes tedium off. The word is lighter than līlā and slightly more human, and putting the two together gives a compound that says she is diverted by her own play. This is not a claim that the world is trivial. The seriousness of it belongs to those who are inside it, which is a different matter from whether it cost her anything.

The four su- names that fill the second line move through the categories of household good fortune. Maṅgala is auspiciousness in the most concrete sense: the good sign, the favourable moment, the thing whose presence makes an undertaking likely to succeed, and sumaṅgalī is also the ordinary word in much of India for a woman whose husband is living. Sukhakarī makes sukha, ease, the state of a well-fitted axle in its socket, which is the old sense underneath the word. Suveṣāḍhyā uses āḍhya, rich in, wealthy in: she is not merely well dressed but abundantly supplied with dress and ornament. That the goddess is worshipped clothed and adorned is not incidental in this liturgy, where robing and ornamenting are two of the standard services offered to her in the rite.

Suvāsinī, the last name, is the one to be careful with. Monier-Williams gives two senses: a woman residing in her father's house, and a courtesy term for a woman whose husband is alive. In the ritual practice of this school the word has a definite referent — the living woman who is seated, fed, and worshipped as the goddess in the suvāsinī pūjā, a rite that the next verse takes up by name. The social category behind it is specific and belongs to a particular order of life, married and not widowed, and a modern reader is better served by seeing that plainly than by translating it into something more comfortable. What is not merely social is the ritual claim: the worship is offered to a person, in the room, and the tradition holds that it arrives where worship offered to the image arrives.
commentary.practice:
This is one of the tidiest verses in the hymn for a reciter, because the names and the metrical feet coincide exactly. Bandhūkakusumaprakhyā is eight syllables and fills the first quarter by itself. Bālā and līlāvinodinī fill the second, two plus six. The whole second line is four names of four syllables each, sumaṅgalī sukhakarī, then suveṣāḍhyā suvāsinī. Nothing straddles a boundary, so the anuṣṭubh will hold its shape as long as you do not hurry.

The danger is the su- run. Four names in a row open with the same syllable, and two of them, sumaṅgalī and sukhakarī, share their shape as well as their opening: four syllables, feminine ī-stem, the same rhythm. Reciters transpose these or repeat one. Fix them by sense rather than by sound — auspiciousness first, then ease, then dress, then the woman herself — and the order will hold.

There are three consonant clusters worth slowing over. In bandhūka the n is fully dental and the dh that follows it is a single aspirated dental, not d plus h; the ū after it is long, and clipping it is the commonest fault in the word. Prakhyā ends the compound with kh plus y, an aspirated guttural running straight into the palatal glide with no vowel between. In sumaṅgalī the ṅ is the guttural nasal, made at the same place as the g that follows, which is why it is written with its own letter; if you say it as an English n the word loses its resonance. Suveṣāḍhyā has the hardest cluster in the verse: ṣ is retroflex, ḍh is a voiced aspirated retroflex, and ḍhy is that sound followed by y. Take it slowly with the tongue curled back for both retroflexes and it becomes stable.

The verse is also a good place to hear the difference between the three sibilants, since ś and ṣ and s all appear: the ś of śobhana-type words is palatal, the ṣ of suveṣā is retroflex, the s of su- is dental and identical to the English s.

For recitation as archanā, where each name is offered in the dative with namaḥ, this verse teaches the two feminine endings side by side. The ā-stems take -āyai: bandhūkakusumaprakhyāyai namaḥ, bālāyai namaḥ, suveṣāḍhyāyai namaḥ. The ī-stems take -yai, with the long ī becoming the glide y: līlāvinodinyai namaḥ, sumaṅgalyai namaḥ, sukhakaryai namaḥ, suvāsinyai namaḥ. Saying the seven in order is about as compact a drill in that alternation as the hymn offers.

As for what the verse asks of the person chanting it, the answer is unusually plain. Everything named here is available at the scale of a house: colour, youth, play, good fortune, ease, good clothes, and a woman in the next room who is to be treated as the goddess. In households that keep this liturgy, the suvāsinī named at the end of the verse is invited, seated, given cloth and food, and honoured before the recitation is closed. The hymn does not descend to the domestic as a concession. It is stating where it expects to be met.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya 11 (from the hymn to Nārāyaṇī)
crossReferences.deva: सर्वमङ्गलमाङ्गल्ये शिवे सर्वार्थसाधिके । शरण्ये त्र्यम्बके गौरि नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते ॥
crossReferences.iast: sarvamaṅgalamāṅgalye śive sarvārthasādhike | śaraṇye tryambake gauri nārāyaṇi namo'stu te ||
crossReferences.translation: You who are the auspiciousness of everything auspicious, you who are Śivā, who accomplish every purpose, in whom refuge is taken, three-eyed, fair one — Nārāyaṇī, homage to you.
crossReferences.relevance: The single best-known verse in Sanskrit on maṅgala, and the background against which sumaṅgalī should be read. It does not say the goddess is auspicious; it says she is the auspiciousness in whatever else is called auspicious, which is what the sahasranāma compresses into one four-syllable name. Its vocative śive also anticipates śrīśivā, five verses further on.

crossReferences.deva: त्वं स्त्री त्वं पुमानसि त्वं कुमार उत वा कुमारी । त्वं जीर्णो दण्डेन वञ्चसि त्वं जातो भवसि विश्वतोमुखः ॥
crossReferences.iast: tvaṃ strī tvaṃ pumān asi tvaṃ kumāra uta vā kumārī | tvaṃ jīrṇo daṇḍena vañcasi tvaṃ jāto bhavasi viśvatomukhaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: You are woman, you are man, you are the boy and the girl as well. You are the old man tottering with his stick; born, you become the one whose faces are turned every way.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest statement of the logic that lets bālā stand beside pūrvajā without contradiction. The Upaniṣad is not saying that the absolute takes turns being these things; it is saying that each of them is a face it wears at full strength. Read this before deciding that calling the mother of the world a girl is a figure of speech.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with the Commentary Saubhāgya-bhāskara of Bhāskararāya
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House / Adyar Library)
references.note: The only full English window onto the commentary that shaped how this hymn has been read since the eighteenth century. The translation is over a century old and the English is stiff, but for any name in this verse it will tell you what the tradition's most influential reader thought was at stake. Treat its etymologies as evidence of a way of reading rather than as philology.

references.title: The Secret of the Three Cities: An Introduction to Hindu Śākta Tantrism
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
references.note: The clearest general account in English of what Śrīvidyā is and how a person enters it, including the graded sequence of mantras through which an initiate passes. Useful here because bālā is not only a word for a girl but the name attached to the mantra many practitioners receive first.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Worth opening for three words in this verse. The entry for bandhūka identifies the plant and its colour; līlā shows how wide the word's range is before theology narrows it; and suvāsinī gives both social senses side by side, which is the honest starting point for a term this loaded.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma (recorded recitation)
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi (HMV / Saregama)
references.note: The recording by which most people in India know the pace of this text. Listen to the second line of this verse in particular: the four su- names are taken as four clean equal beats, which is exactly the discipline that keeps a reciter from sliding them together.
